questions.stem: What does Rule 7(c) of the Collision Regulations say about assumptions?
options: Assumptions shall not be made on the basis of scanty information, especially scanty radar information
Assumptions may be made if the radar shows a target for more than one minute
Assumptions about other vessels are allowed if the bearing is changing
Assumptions are to be recorded in the log before acting
questions.explanation: Rule 7(c) forbids assumptions on scanty information, and singles out radar information. A single sighting is scanty, which is why systematic observation or plotting is needed (Rule 7(b)).

questions.stem: In a six-minute radar plot, what are R, M and the DRM line?
options: R is own ship, M is the target and DRM is the course made good
R is range, M is bearing and DRM is the direction of the wind
R is the radar horizon, M is the maximum range and DRM is the drift
R is the first plotted position, M is the position six minutes later, and the DRM line is the line through them extended past own ship
questions.explanation: R and M are the two plotted positions of the target six minutes apart. The line through them is the direction of relative motion line (DRM), the path the target appears to follow relative to your ship.

questions.stem: How is the closest point of approach (CPA) read from a relative plot?
options: As the distance from R to M
As the range at the second sighting
As the shortest distance from own ship at the centre to the DRM line
As the bearing of the target at the first sighting
questions.explanation: CPA is how close the target will pass if both vessels hold course and speed, which is the perpendicular distance from the centre of the plot to the DRM line. RM is a movement, not a clearance.

questions.stem: On a relative plot the DRM line passes exactly through the centre. What does that mean?
options: The target is stationary
The CPA is zero and a collision will occur if neither vessel changes course or speed
The target will pass at the radar's minimum range
The plot must be repeated because the radar is defective
questions.explanation: A line through the centre means the target is heading for your position, a collision course. A stationary object plots a line parallel to your course instead.

questions.stem: On a six-minute plot, the target moves 0.85 nm along the line from R to M. What is the relative speed?
options: 8.5 knots
0.85 knots
5.1 knots
85 knots
questions.explanation: Six minutes is one tenth of an hour, so relative speed in knots is the distance in six minutes times 10: 0.85 × 10 = 8.5 knots. Multiplying by 6 gives 5.1, a common slip.

questions.stem: A target on a steady bearing is at 6.0 nm, then 5.4 nm six minutes later. What is the time to CPA, measured from the second plot, if neither vessel changes?
options: 9 minutes
36 minutes
5.4 minutes
54 minutes
questions.explanation: The range fell 0.6 nm in 6 minutes, so relative speed is 6 knots. With CPA zero, the remaining distance is 5.4 nm, so TCPA = 5.4 ÷ 6 = 0.9 hours = 54 minutes.

questions.stem: Over six minutes a target's bearing changes from 045° to 043° relative while the range falls from 6.0 nm to 4.8 nm. What is the best conclusion?
options: The 2° change shows it will pass clear, so no action is needed
A bearing change under 5° cannot be measured, so the target should be ignored
It is closing with an almost steady bearing, so risk of collision should be treated as existing and the plot continued
Only a change of range matters, and bearing is irrelevant
questions.explanation: Rule 7(d)(i) deems risk to exist if the compass bearing does not appreciably change. Here the plot gives a CPA of about 0.8 nm with under half an hour to go, so it is not a safe pass. Keep plotting and act early.

questions.stem: A plot gives a good CPA, but the target then alters course. What is the effect on the plot?
options: The plot remains valid because radar compensates automatically
The plot is no longer valid, because it assumes both vessels hold course and speed
Only the TCPA changes, not the CPA
The plot becomes more accurate with each alteration
questions.explanation: A relative plot assumes both vessels keep course and speed. An alteration by either changes the direction of relative motion, so a new plot is needed. A third plot point off the line is the clue that something changed.

questions.stem: A buoy is plotted over six minutes while your ship steams steadily ahead. How does its DRM line compare with your own course?
options: It runs parallel to your course, in the opposite direction, because only your ship is moving
It runs through the centre of the plot
It is perpendicular to your course
It does not move at all
questions.explanation: A fixed object appears to move relative to you at your own speed, along a line parallel to your course and back down the screen. That is how a plot reveals a stationary target.

questions.stem: At the first sighting an echo is at 8.0 nm and at the second, six minutes later, 6.8 nm, bearing steady. The mate says the target is probably passing clear. Which reply is best?
options: Agreed, because the target is still more than 6 miles away
Agreed, because a steady bearing means the target is keeping its distance
No view is possible until the target is within 2 nm
The range fell 1.2 nm in six minutes, relative speed is 12 knots, the bearing is steady, and CPA is near zero with about 34 minutes to go
questions.explanation: A steady bearing with a falling range is a collision course. The range fell 1.2 nm in 6 minutes, a relative speed of 12 knots, so TCPA is 6.8 ÷ 12 = 0.57 hours, about 34 minutes. The steady bearing is the warning, not the remaining distance.
